title: Cambodia’s NGO Sector Is Collapsing. Does It Matter?
author: Louise Coventry
text:
A dusty road in Treak village, Siem Reap province, Cambodia.
Credit: Depositphotos
From the early 1990s through the early 2010s, Cambodia hosted one of the most vibrant, generously funded, and unchecked civil society ecosystems in Southeast Asia. Former Prime Minister Hun Sen once famously referred to the country as a “heaven for NGOs.” And indeed, up to 6,100 registered non-government organizations (NGOs) and associations have been able to flourish, including about 3,450 NGOs and 2,650 other civil society associations. This number of NGOs is very high by global standards, by one count making up the second highest number per capita in the world after Rwanda.A confluence of disasters has changed all that. The heyday for NGOs effectively started closing following the 2013 national elections, when the ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP) faced a major electoral threat and began systematically dismantling the public sphere. Viewing NGOs as a vehicle for hostile foreign-backed “color revolutions,” the Cambodian government introduced a restrictive and controversial Law on Associations and Non-Governmental Organizations in 2015. It also began to use tax audits, lawsuits, and political pressure – such as monitoring or disturbing civil society meetings, refusing to give permission for activities, and other coercive tactics – to restrict the sector.[...]
